spans.sentence: In the 2026 State of Supply Chain Sustainability report, 83 percent of respondents rate sustainability as important or very important to long-term business success, the highest level in the report's seven-year history.

According to the 2026 State of Supply Chain Sustainability report from the MIT Sustainable Supply Chain Lab , which surveyed 1,810 supply chain professionals across 91 countries, 83 percent rate sustainability as important or very important to long-term business success, the highest level in the report's seven-year history.

While 59 percent of respondents report becoming more committed to sustainability following recent U.S. policy shifts that deprioritize environmental concerns, the same organizations are being forced to compromise those commitments.
Beyond tariffs, more than eight in 10 respondents across North America, Europe, and Asia agree that ongoing geopolitical conflict is reducing the effectiveness of their organization’s climate action.

Among companies with publicly stated sustainability goals, only 51 percent have established a formal cross-functional sustainability team, which is the governance structure most strongly associated with embedding sustainability into daily decisions.
In addition, only 33 percent place sustainability oversight at the board level.
Companies with formal cross-functional teams report sustainability is "frequently or always" built into decisions 57 percent of the time.
Where responsibility sits in a single function, that drops to 13 percent — a 44-point gap illustrating the return on governance investment.

Sustainability is embedding most deeply where companies make daily operational choices: transportation and logistics (39 percent), procurement (35 percent), warehousing (34 percent), and product design (33 percent).
Seventy-eight percent of North American organizations report current use of AI in sustainability initiatives, and 87 percent of adopters report positive impact on sustainability goals.
Eighty-six percent have reduced material waste, 81 percent have reduced energy use, and 63 percent use AI to estimate missing supplier emissions data.
However, among mature agentic AI users, only 53 percent report a reduction in total greenhouse gas emissions.

Among advanced and fully automated warehouses using AI, 78 percent report higher energy use since implementing AI, and 76 percent report higher waste, yet only 24 percent use AI-driven real-time monitoring to track environmental consequences.
However, 43 percent of fleets still operate mostly or entirely on conventional diesel and only 8 percent have completed a full transition to low-emission energy.
The divergence between regions reveals why: In Europe, 84 percent of freight companies report that recent policy changes have positively affected decarbonization strategy.
In North America, only 44 percent do.
For example, battery-electric vehicles are at scale in 60 percent of European companies, but only 36 percent in North America.
The report reveals that one bright spot has emerged in Scope 3, or indirect, emissions collaboration.
Participation in joint supplier engagement and decarbonization programs surged from 31 to 58 percent in a single year.
In addition, partnerships to manage shared suppliers' emissions more than doubled, from 23 to 55 percent.
The share working entirely alone collapsed from 18 to 6 percent.
Robinson Foundation, Breakthrough, and CO 2 AI and Dassault Systèmes, reveals that companies are recognizing that Scope 3 cannot be solved in isolation.

Over the past five years, the price of thought — the cost for an AI to hit a particular benchmark score — has fallen 13× per year.

It seems to be a faster pace than any other transformative technology has matched: it’s four times faster than DNA sequencing, six times faster than compute, 18 times faster than lithium batteries, and (in the century up to 1973) 54 times faster than electricity.
We estimate that for an average cost of 30 cents per question, it could achieve a 75% score on GPQA Diamond , a multiple-choice exam covering PhD-level physics, chemistry, and biology.
It scored just as well — for four hundredths of a penny per question ($0.0004).
That is a 725-fold drop in the price of thought in under 18 months, equivalent to the sticker price on a new car falling from $50,000 to $69 in only a year and a half.
Prices fall 13× per year; fastest soon after they release

Last month we introduced the first GPT‑6 models for paid customers and today we're bringing that next generation of intelligence to more people with a new GPT‑6 model built for more than 1.2 billion people who use ChatGPT each week.

GPT‑6 in ChatGPT introduces Intelligent UI, a new capability that allows ChatGPT to answer quickly with fully interactive user interfaces that make everyday answers more visual, make learning complex topics easier and that can quickly create a tool to solve a task right in the moment.

We’ve trained GPT‑6 to compose responses using text, visuals and interactive elements, choosing how they fit together based on your question.
With Intelligent UI, we gave GPT‑6 the freedom to create the most useful interface for each question, while keeping the experience fast and familiar across web and mobile.
GPT‑6 learned to use the component library and make good design decisions, including how to organize information clearly, when to use interactivity, and when a simple text response is enough.
With GPT‑6, we’re also making it possible for ChatGPT to begin answering while it continues to think.
GPT‑5.6 Instant

In an internal evaluation of high-value, everyday agentic tasks, GPT‑6 Extra High is able to begin answering in the same amount of time as GPT‑5.6 Medium while achieving a better overall score than GPT‑5.6 Extra High.
For questions that need web search, GPT‑6 Instant starts answering 44% sooner, on average, than GPT‑5.6 Instant.
GPT‑6 also improves the quality of answers that require web search.
In an internal evaluation of difficult problems, GPT‑6 correctly addressed the key aspect of the user’s question more often than GPT‑5.6.
Deploying GPT‑6 safely

GPT‑6 makes progress in each of these areas, building on several of Astra’s safety advances to better resist attempts to bypass its safety training, follow safeguards, and be clearer about what it can and can’t do relative to GPT‑5.6 Sol.
In adversarial testing, GPT‑6 showed stronger resistance to attempts to bypass its safety training, particularly attacks that adapt across multiple turns.
GPT‑6 is also trained to respond safely in higher-risk scenarios while avoiding unnecessary refusals of harmless requests.
GPT‑6 is better at recognizing and communicating the limits of its own capabilities, including when it lacks the information or tools needed to answer.
